item.title: AVS and complementary services in Canton Bern
item.description: How the calculation of the AVS pension works in the Canton of Bern: mandatory contributions, contribution gaps, supplementary benefits and coverage of the minimum living allowance.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - AVS contributions 5.3% for employees (total 10.6% with employer) - Contribution gaps reduce retirement pension amount - Supplementary benefits supplement the minimum living standard for retirees - Compensation fund of the Canton of Bern manages payment administration
## Key facts - **What**: AVS pension calculated on contributions paid + supplements from supplementary benefits - Where: Canton of Bern with cantonal compensation fund - Who: Employees, employers, UFAS (Federal Social Insurance Office) - When: Payments throughout the entire working career; pension upon reaching ordinary retirement age - Employee contribution: 5.3% on gross salary - Total contribution: 10.6% (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer)
### The first pillar in the Canton of Bern
In the Canton of Bern, as in the rest of Switzerland, the Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS) represents the first pillar of the national pension system. The mandatory contribution for employees is set at 5.3% on the salary, while the employer pays another 5.3% share, bringing the total to 10.6% of the coordinated salary. These payments feed into the calculation of the future AVS pension at the time of retirement and form the basis for access to insurance benefits.
The cantonal compensation fund of the Canton of Bern manages the administration of these payments and maintains the contribution accounting of each insured person. A crucial role to ensure that the contributions paid during the professional career are correctly recorded, accounted for, and subsequently used to calculate the pension. Without this precise administration at the cantonal level, it would not be possible to determine with certainty the amount due to each retiree.
Contribution gaps — periods during which no AVS contributions are made — directly affect the amount of the future pension. A career with interruptions, change of profession, periods of unemployment, or other situations that result in the absence of contributions, determines a lower total of accumulated payments and thus a lower AVS pension compared to someone with a continuous career without interruptions. These gaps are recorded in the accounting and remain permanent in the pension calculation.
For this reason, in the Canton of Bern and in other Swiss cantons, supplementary benefits come into play: forms of pension income integration that are activated when the AVS pension, although correctly calculated, does not reach the legal minimum living standard. Supplementary benefits cover the difference between what is received as an AVS pension and the minimum guaranteed income threshold, allowing retirees to have adequate resources for their subsistence. ### How to calculate the AVS pension in the Canton of Bern
The AVS pension is determined based on the total contributions paid throughout one's working career. The more contributions accumulated and the longer the career, the higher the pension amount at the ordinary retirement age. In the Canton of Bern, as in other cantons, the calculation is made according to uniform federal formulas; you can consult the guide on [AVS, LPP and pension](nav:pension) for more details on the calculation mechanism. The local administration of the compensation fund ensures that the contribution data is accurate and up-to-date throughout one's professional life.
A continuous working career without gaps allows for the accumulation of the maximum annual contributions, thus optimizing the future pension. However, many people face interruptions in their work career: periods of unemployment, geographical transfers, sector changes, leaves for family or personal reasons, or years in which the income is below the minimum contribution threshold. Each of these situations generates a contribution gap, i.e., a year or period in which no AVS contribution is paid or the payments are below the required minimum.
### Concrete Impact of Gaps on Pension Calculation
One of the critical points in the Swiss pension system is how contribution gaps are handled in the pension calculation. Unlike other systems that apply forms of automatic recovery, Switzerland considers gaps as empty periods in the computation of accumulated contributions; these remain in the accounting and reduce the total number of years with full contributions. A worker who accumulates, for example, 5 years of gaps during a 45-year career will see their AVS pension calculated on 40 years of contributions instead of 45, with a proportional reduction in the amount due.
In the Canton of Bern, insured individuals can receive a detailed extract of the contribution accounting from their compensation fund to verify how many years of contributions have been accumulated and if there are specific gaps. Consulting this accounting is essential for planning retirement and understanding if it will be necessary to resort to complementary benefits to fill the gap between the calculated pension and the minimum living standard.
### The Role of Complementary Benefits in the Minimum Living Standard
Complementary benefits intervene to fill the gap between the calculated AVS pension (even if reduced by gaps) and the guaranteed minimum living standard. The minimum living standard represents the minimum amount of income necessary to live decently in Switzerland and varies according to the canton and individual situation (single, couples, with dependents, etc.). If a retiree in the Canton of Bern receives an AVS pension below this threshold, complementary benefits provide the necessary integration. This mechanism ensures that no retiree falls below the legal minimum living standard, regardless of the contribution gaps accumulated during their professional career.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to check your AVS contributions with the Bern compensation fund
To plan your retirement in the Canton of Bern, the first step is to check your contribution statement with the cantonal compensation fund. The Bern compensation fund provides contribution statements upon request, detailing the years of contributions paid and any gaps in your work history. This document is essential for calculating the estimated amount of your AVS pension at retirement.
The check can be done directly at the compensation fund offices or, in many cases, through the online portals provided by the entity itself. Insured individuals have the right to receive a statement of their contribution data regularly; consulting these statements is essential to identify any errors or omissions and to request timely corrections before retirement. It is advisable to check your [salary calculator](nav:calculator) annually to ensure that your contribution data is correct and up-to-date.
### Procedure to request supplementary benefits in the Canton of Bern
If the analysis of the statement shows that the future AVS pension will not be sufficient for the guaranteed minimum living standard, it is advisable to inform yourself in advance about the procedures to access supplementary benefits in the Canton of Bern. Supplementary benefits are not automatically granted but require a formal application in which you document your income, assets, and overall financial situation.
The application can be submitted to the compensation fund or directly to the cantonal office responsible for supplementary benefits. You will need to provide complete documentation of your financial situation: official tax returns, bank statements, information on real estate and movable assets. The fund will then conduct a thorough assessment of the situation and determine the amount of the supplement due based on federal and cantonal criteria. Supplementary benefits start from the moment the application is formally accepted.
### Tools, deadlines, and next steps
Those approaching retirement in the Canton of Bern should plan well in advance, at least 12-18 months before, to avoid surprises and ensure timely access to all available benefits. It is important to coordinate the communication of your AVS pension with the competent cantonal authorities, verify that the statement is complete and accurate, and inform yourself about the specific deadlines for submitting applications for supplementary benefits.
To simulate your gross amount and calculate the contributions made, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). For tax details and documentation from the previous year, consult the [tax return](nav:tax-return). For more detailed information on AVS, LPP, and pension calculation methods, visit the [Pension and Benefits](nav:pension) section available on the site. Contact the Bern compensation fund directly to verify deadlines, forms, and specific procedures related to your case.

## Key facts - What: Forced closure of company accounts for mining activities. - When: Q3 2024. - Where: Lugano and Canton Ticino. - Who: Double-licensed startups (real estate and mining). - Impact: Total stagnation of cash flows.
The story of S. reflects a deep fracture in the Swiss financial landscape. His company, active in real estate and Bitcoin mining, clashes with the strict compliance protocol of cantonal and national banks. Mining, conceived as a reserve of strategic liquidity, has become the Achilles heel of its banking operations.
Technically, mining is based on ASIC hardware. With an investment of 130,000 francs, S. generates about 0.1 BTC per month (current value of about 6,500 USD), against energy expenses of 5,000 USD. The margin, albeit volatile, is traceable. However, banks apply de-risking policies that do not distinguish between illicit activities and transparent industrial mining.
> “I've always handled everything transparently, but the banks closed the accounts without appeal, making it impossible to pay suppliers and salaries.”
The paradox is exacerbated by the law ## Practical Analysis
The difficulties encountered by S. are not an isolated case but reflect a systemic criticality that affects the entire Swiss ecosystem. Lars Schlichting, an expert blockchain lawyer, confirms that the banking blockade does not only affect mining but stifles the entire innovative entrepreneurship. Often, banks open the constitution account, necessary for the deposit of the minimum share capital of 100,000 francs for a SA, but deny the transformation into an operational account. This stalemate forces startups to migrate to foreign neobanks, such as Revolut or Wise, weakening domestic financial control.
> "Banks are afraid of what is not traditional, inadvertently favoring the flight of capital abroad."

Lorenzo Ambrosini, director of the Agire Foundation, emphasizes that the lack of a financial history makes young companies high risk for traditional institutions. The situation is particularly tense in innovation hubs such as Ticino or the Canton of Zug, where the concentration of cryptographic companies is high.
📊 Practical Scenario: The Cost of Exclusion
A startup that does not obtain a bank account in Switzerland within 30 days of its constitution suffers operational delays that can cost between 5,000 and 15,000 francs in extra legal consultations. In comparison, a startup that accesses traditional bank credit incurs annual management costs of approximately 1,200 francs.

- Prepare a detailed business plan with cash flow projections for 24 months. - Certify compliance with AML (Anti-Money Laundering) according to the Money Laundering Act (MLA) in force since January 1, 2023. - Present a clear governance structure with identifiable economic beneficiaries. - Evaluate cantonal banks with public service mandates, often more inclined to dialogue than private institutions.
⚠️ Regulatory Comparison
While FINMA has updated the guidelines on digital client identification, many banks apply even more restrictive *de-risking* policies, refusing a priori sectors with high reputational risk to avoid sanctions related to international compliance.

Analyze the technical reasons: often the problem lies in a risk profile that does not comply with the FINMA standards updated to 2021 on the fight against money laundering. Consult a legal expert in Swiss banking law to draw up an opinion on the compliance of your transactions. Explore local alternatives such as innovation-oriented cantonal banks (e.g. Zug or Geneva) or specialist institutions such as Sygnum or SEBA, which offer dedicated accounts with initial deposit thresholds often exceeding CHF 50,000.
> Document transparency is the best defense against unilateral closure of accounts.
Document every operation with Swiss precision. If you operate in Zug's Crypto Valley, make sure your audit is certified by local auditors. Keep an up-to-date record of transactions to avoid budget holds.

item.title: Buying a house in Bern: prices, mortgage and taxes
item.description: Practical guide to buying real estate in the Canton of Bern: transfer tax, notary fees, own funds required and mortgage loan sustainability.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Transfer tax: cantonal tax on the buyer in the Canton of Bern - Own funds: minimum 20% of the property value required by Swiss banks - Notary fees: 1-2% of the purchase price according to cantonal rates - LAMal mandatory within 3 months of becoming a new resident in the canton
## Key facts - **What**: Purchasing a property in the Canton of Bern with tax and procedural obligations - Where: Canton of Bern (Central Switzerland) - Who: Buyer, notary, bank, Bernese cantonal administration - When: At the time of purchase and signing of the deed - Minimum own funds: Approximately 20% of the estimated value of the property
When you buy a house in the Canton of Bern, the total cost goes far beyond the advertised purchase price. In addition to paying for the property, you must consider the transfer tax, notary fees, cadastral documentation, and administrative costs. At the same time, if you are a new resident in the canton, you automatically enter the Swiss tax system at three levels (federal, cantonal, and municipal) and are obligated to enroll in health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months. The Swiss banking system also imposes strict rules for accessing a mortgage: own funds equal to at least 20% of the property value are required. Understanding these elements is essential to realistically assess whether the purchase is sustainable.
### Transfer tax: a cantonal tax
The transfer tax (also known as inheritance tax or property transfer tax) is a cantonal tax — not federal. In the Canton of Bern, it is regulated by its own cantonal law, which sets the rates and procedures. The tax applies to the transfer of property ownership and is calculated based on the declared sale price.
Each Swiss canton has a different rate: the same house would pay different amounts if purchased in Ticino, Zurich, Geneva, or Bern. This difference is structural in the Swiss system: each canton has fiscal sovereignty over this matter. Federal competence does not come into play. Those who buy in Bern pay the tax to the cantonal administration. Registration with the municipal cadastre is carried out by the notary in charge of the signing, who ensures compliance with all federal and cantonal regulations.
### Own funds and mortgage sustainability
The Swiss banking system requires minimum own funds equal to 20% of the estimated value of the property. If the house costs CHF 500,000, you must have at least CHF 100,000 in own funds (savings, inheritance, loans from relatives); the remaining 80% is financed by the bank through a mortgage. This is a well-established rule in Switzerland and applied by the vast majority of banks.
Higher own funds (30%, 40% or more) improve mortgage conditions: lower interest rates and easier approval. The bank evaluates the sustainability of the mortgage according to a rigorous criterion: the annual property burden (mortgage installment, interest, insurance, maintenance) should not exceed 33% of the gross family income. An annual income of CHF 120,000 could support a maximum annual burden of CHF 40,000.
### LAMal and enrollment obligation
If you buy a house and become a resident in the Canton of Bern, you are obligated to enroll in health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months. It is not a tax but a mandatory private insurance: the premium is individual (per capita), not calculated on the family. Premiums vary based on canton, age, and chosen deductible (CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500 annually). The Canton of Bern applies cantonal subsidies for those with income below certain limits, reducing the cost of coverage. ## Three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal, and municipal
Anyone who buys a house and resides in Bern enters the Swiss tax system, which is structured in three levels: direct federal tax (DFT), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. The DFT is set by the Confederation and applied uniformly throughout the country. The cantonal tax is regulated by the Canton of Bern with its own rates. The municipal tax varies from municipality to municipality within the canton: each municipality applies a multiplier to the cantonal base, thus creating different rates even a few kilometers apart.
The structure is complex, but it offers advantages for those who own a property: the interest on the first mortgage (covered by personal funds) is generally deductible from cantonal and municipal taxes. This deductibility reduces the tax burden for the decade (or more) of mortgage repayment. If you pay CHF 20,000 in interest per year, the amount is subtracted from the taxable income in the canton of Bern, thus lowering the tax due at the cantonal and municipal levels. The deduction does not apply to the federal tax.
### Calculating sustainability: the debt-to-income ratio
Before granting a mortgage, the Swiss bank calculates the 'housing burden' — the sum of all costs related to the house (annual mortgage payment + interest, fire insurance, estimated maintenance, municipal property taxes). This burden divided by the annual gross income should not exceed 33%. If your family earns CHF 150,000 gross per year, the maximum sustainable burden is CHF 49,500 annually.
In practice, a bank calculates the maximum mortgage based on this criterion. A client with a high income but a very expensive property might not get the desired mortgage because the burden exceeds the threshold. Some institutions apply slightly different parameters (31%-35%), but the concept remains the same: to protect the client from unsustainable debt.
### Mortgage interest and tax planning
The interest on the first mortgage reduces cantonal and municipal taxes, but not federal taxes. This is an important element of planning: as you repay the mortgage and the interest decreases, your cantonal/municipal taxation increases (because the deductions decrease). After 20-25 years, when the mortgage is almost paid off, the tax burden on the property is zero (you no longer have interest to deduct), but at the same time, you no longer pay mortgage installments. This is a natural dynamic of the Swiss system.
Some owners maintain a small portion of the mortgage even after they could have paid it off, to take advantage of the deductibility of interest and invest the savings elsewhere. This is not a common strategy, but it is legal and used in certain contexts of asset planning.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Practical procedure: steps from interest to notarial deed
Phase 1: Research and cadastral survey
When you identify a property of interest in the Canton of Bern, contact the local Land Registry Office (Ufficio del Registro fondiario) to verify the legal situation: whether the property is free from encumbrances, mortgages, or charges. You can request a cadastral survey online or at the office. The notary in charge of the sale will make this verification on your behalf, but it is useful to do it in advance.
Phase 2: Bank consultation and pre-mortgage offer
Consult 2-3 banks to obtain a pre-offer (letter of intent) on the mortgage. Provide the estimated value of the property, your available own funds, the last 2-3 pay slips, and a tax return. The bank performs an independent valuation of the property and calculates the maximum mortgage according to sustainability criteria. A pre-offer is generally valid for 30-60 days.
Phase 3: Negotiation with the seller and notarial commitment
Negotiate the price with the seller. Once an agreement is reached, the notary in charge of the sale prepares the preliminary sale agreement (or compromise) and any deposit. The notary is generally chosen by one of the parties (often the seller, who pays for it), but remains impartial.
Phase 4: Financing and signing before the notary
The bank completes the application and grants the final mortgage. The notary prepares the sale deed (rogito) indicating the price, conditions, mortgage, and all cadastral data. You and the seller are summoned together (or separately, at the notary's discretion) to sign the deed. The signatures must be authenticated before the notary. The notary collects the funds (yours + those of the mortgage) in a blocked account, in your name, until the transfer is registered.
Phase 5: Cadastral registration and property transfer
After signing, the notary sends the deed to the Land Registry Office (cadastral) for registration. The date of entry is the official date of property transfer. The notary receives confirmation of registration and communicates it to you and the bank. The bank registers the mortgage of its interest.
Phase 6: Health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months
If you did not have previous health insurance in the Canton of Bern, enroll within 3 months of the property transfer date (or in any case from the date of change of residence). Choose an authorized health insurance fund in the canton. It is not mandatory to change funds if you already had insurance, but rates may vary by residence and canton, so check with our [LAMal comparator](nav:health).
Phase 7: Registration with the municipality and tax declaration
Register with the municipality of your place of residence in Bern within 14 days of the transfer. Report the new real estate property. Prepare the [cantonal and municipal tax return](nav:tax-return) for the fiscal year in which you purchase: you must indicate the real estate property, the mortgage amount, the interest paid (deductible), and other asset data.
## Critical deadlines and useful tools
Within 3 months of changing residence: LAMal registration. Within 14 days: registration with the municipality. By the end of the fiscal year: cantonal/municipal tax declaration. Use the [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) of Frontaliere Ticino to evaluate your tax burden once you have acquired the property. Consult the notary specialized in real estate law at least 4-6 weeks before signing to avoid delays.
**Next steps**: Contact a notary specialized in real estate sales in your municipality of residence in Bern. Request 2-3 pre-mortgage offers from different banks. Check if you are eligible for cantonal subsidy programs for LAMal premiums (the Canton of Bern applies reductions for incomes below specific thresholds). Start today with our [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to plan your real estate purchase.

item.title: Apprenticeship and training in Canton Thurgau
item.description: Practical guide to the apprenticeship system in Switzerland: how to find an apprenticeship, learn about the apprentice's rights and the training contract.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship in Switzerland: dual system (internship + vocational school) - Duration: 2-4 years, with federal certificate at the end - Apprentice rights: contractual protection (CO), social security, cantonal minimum wage
## Key facts - **What**: Dual apprenticeship system in Switzerland (company internship + vocational school) - When: Duration 2-4 years, final exam with federal certificate - Where: Canton of Thurgau and other 25 cantons (federally coordinated system) - Who: Young people after compulsory schooling, craft/commercial/service companies - Legislation: Rights and duties regulated by the Code of Obligations (CO) arts. 344a-360 - Social Security: AVS/AI 5.3% (employee), mandatory LAMal, LPP for eligible by age
Apprenticeship in Switzerland represents a pillar of the national vocational training system. In the Canton of Thurgau, as in the other twenty-six Swiss cantons, the system follows federal regulations regarding workers' rights, social security, and contractual protection, coordinated by the Confederation.
The Swiss model is based on a dual system: the young apprentice works in a company to gain practical experience while receiving theoretical instruction at a public vocational school (usually one or two days a week). This approach allows the apprentice to earn a salary during training. Apprenticeship is intended for those who have completed compulsory schooling and wish to pursue a technical, craft, commercial, or service profession.
The duration varies depending on the profession: usually two, three, or four years. At the end, the apprentice takes a final exam that includes practical, theoretical, and sometimes work project tests. Those who pass the exam receive a federal vocational training certificate, recognized nationally and internationally.
### How to find an internship
The search for an internship is mainly done through national online portals, regional chambers of commerce, vocational schools, and direct contacts with companies. In the Canton of Thurgau, the competent cantonal office provides information on companies offering positions, available training cycles, and application deadlines. Internship offers are typically published from September to November for the following year. Candidates must prepare an application with a CV, cover letter, and school certificates, sent directly to the interested companies.
Professional orientation, provided by middle schools and cantonal counseling services, helps young people identify the most suitable path. Some companies require a preliminary interview or a trial internship before signing the final contract. ### The internship contract and the rights of the apprentice
The internship contract is a legal document that regulates the relationship between the apprentice and the company. According to the Swiss Code of Obligations (CO) articles 344a-360, the contract must contain essential information: the duration of the internship, the title of the profession, the weekly working hours, the gross salary, the paid holidays and the duties and rights of both parties. The contract must be signed before the start of the internship, and a copy must be given to the apprentice.
The apprentice is entitled to a minimum wage. Although Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage, many cantons, including the canton of Thurgau, have set minimum amounts for apprentices. The amounts vary depending on the level of training (first, second, third, fourth year) and the professional sector. For specific amounts in the canton of Thurgau, consult the cantonal vocational training office or the professional association of the sector.
During the apprenticeship, the apprentice is covered by federal social security. Mandatory contributions include:
- **AVS/AI (old age, disability, unemployment)**: 5.3% of the apprentice's salary, 10.6% overall (inclusive of the employer's contribution) - Health insurance (LAMal): mandatory by federal law for all residents, privately contracted with health insurance funds, with variable individual premiums
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure: Starting an apprenticeship
The search for an internship usually follows a fixed annual calendar. Below are the main steps:
1. **June-August**: Search and application. Consult online portals for internship offers at the national and regional levels, prepare a CV and a cover letter, and send applications to companies offering the desired profession.
2. September-November: Selection interviews. Participate in meetings with selected companies, demonstrate interest, technical skills, and professional motivation.
3. December-January: Contract signing. Once you receive the offer, sign the internship contract before the indicated deadline (usually end of January).
4. Following August: Official start of the internship. Begin the dual path at the company and the vocational school.
5. During the internship: Regularly check your rights (salary, vacation, pension, safety) and comply with contractual obligations.
### Checking salary, pension, and rights
During the apprenticeship, it is important to periodically check that the gross salary is in accordance with the cantonal minimum amounts, that the pension contributions (AVS/AI, LAMal, LAINF, LPP) are correctly deducted, and that the employer respects contractual rights. In case of doubts or disputes, the cantonal office of vocational training offers support and advice.
To estimate the net monthly salary of an apprentice in the Canton of Thurgau, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). To better understand your social security obligations [AVS/AI/LPP](nav:pension), consult the dedicated guides or contact the cantonal office.
Don't miss the opportunity to build a solid career in Switzerland: subscribe to the Frontaliere Ticino newsletter to receive monthly updates on Swiss tax, pension, and labor market news.

item.title: Permit L short duration Thurgau: extension and renewal
item.description: The L permit allows you to work in Switzerland for periods of up to one year. Find out how it works in Thurgau, the extension conditions and the switch to the B permit.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Permit L valid for up to 1 year for work in Switzerland - Renewable with agreement between employer and employee - Transition to Permit B possible if the employment relationship continues - Tied to the employer and the duration of the contract
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term Permit L (Bewilligung L) - Maximum duration: 1 year, renewable - Where: Canton of Thurgau (cantonal administration for approval) - Who: Foreign citizens employed by Swiss employers - Renewal: On joint request, if the employment relationship continues
The short-term Permit L is the first step for those intending to work in Switzerland. It allows foreign citizens to work for periods of up to one year, renewable. Nationally, the Permit L is regulated by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) and federal ordinances on the labor market.
In Thurgau, as in the other 25 Swiss cantons, the administrative management of Permit L is the responsibility of the competent cantonal authority. There is no separate Thurgau Permit L — rather, the canton applies federal standards with its own procedures and decision times.
### Maximum validity and constraints
The maximum validity of the Permit L is set at 1 year. Unlike the Permit B (residence, renewable every 5 years), the Permit L is strictly linked to three factors: the specific employer, the type of work activity, and the duration of the employment contract. You cannot change employers without a new permit application. If the contract ends, the right of residence ceases.
The actual duration of the permit may be less than one year if the employment contract is shorter. For example, a 6-month contract results in a 6-month Permit L.
### Who can obtain it in Thurgau
The Permit L is primarily intended for foreign workers hired for temporary, seasonal, or short-term projects. In Thurgau, access depends on the sector: some areas (agriculture, catering, construction) have streamlined procedures for seasonal Permit L; others require a Swiss labor market analysis (preliminary check) to verify that no local workforce is available.
To apply for a Permit L in Thurgau, the employer must submit an application to the cantonal migration service within crucial deadlines: normally, the request must be submitted at least 4 weeks before the start of employment. ### Extension and renewal of the L permit
The extension of the L permit in Thurgau is done upon joint request: the employer and the employee must agree to continue the employment relationship and submit a new application to the cantonal migration service. It is not automatic. The renewal application must be received BEFORE the expiry of the current permit.
In practice, if your L permit expires on December 31, 2026, and you wish to continue with the same employer, both parties must sign and submit the renewal forms at least 30 days in advance — times may vary depending on the workload of the cantonal office. Once expired, there are no tolerance extensions: the right of residence ceases immediately.
Each renewal restarts the count: after the first L permit of 1 year, a second L permit is possible. However, if the employment lasts more than 2 years, it is more convenient to transition to a B permit, which offers greater job stability and flexibility.
### Transition from L permit to B permit
The B permit (residence) represents a subsequent step in the progression of Swiss residence permits. It is renewable every 5 years (instead of 1 year) and offers greater flexibility in changing employers. The transition from L to B is not automatic: it must be requested from the cantonal migration service and evaluated based on stable criteria.
In Thurgau, the transition L → B is granted if the employment continues stably (permanent contract or at least 2 years of continuous employment), the employer supports the request, and there are no obstacles to residence (unjustified absences, serious infractions, etc.). The B permit allows you to stay in Switzerland even if you change employers (notifying the new employment), and opens access to broader social benefits (housing subsidies, tax deductions, etc.) at the cantonal level.
### Constraints related to the employer
An important limitation of the L permit: it is tied to the employer declared in the application. If the employment ends prematurely, the permit lapses. You cannot transfer the L permit to a new employer — you must let the first permit expire and apply for a new one.
This restriction protects the Swiss labor market but limits the worker's mobility. If you find new employment before the expiry, you must terminate the first contract, wait for the possible expiry of the L permit (or request its early cancellation), and then submit a new application with the new employer.
In Thurgau, the migration service communicates directly with the employer to verify the persistence of employment and compliance with Swiss labor market regulations.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How to request the L permit in Thurgau: step-by-step
Phase 1: Preparation (1-2 weeks before the start of work) 1. The employer collects documents: signed employment contract, copy of the candidate's passport, declaration of compliance with wage and safety regulations. 2. Check with the cantonal migration service whether the sector requires prior labor market assessment (common for construction, catering, domestic services). 3. Fill out the official application form (downloadable from the official cantonal website turgovia.ch or requested from the office).
Phase 2: Submission of the application The application must reach the competent service at least 4 weeks before the start date of work (to allow for processing). Processing times vary: generally 2-4 weeks for non-critical sectors, up to 6-8 weeks if prior assessment is necessary.
**Phase 3: Processing and approval** The cantonal office verifies the documentation, contacts the employer for confirmations, and issues the L permit (physical document or digital clearance). There are no federal administrative costs for issuing the L permit, although the canton may charge minimal administrative fees (variable by canton).
Phase 4: Registration with the Municipality Once the L permit is received, the worker must register with the Municipality or the Population Office of the place of residence within 14 days of arrival. This step is mandatory to access basic services (LAMal, bank account, insurance).
### Documents required for the application - Valid passport (or ID card for EU/EFTA citizens) - Original signed employment contract (duration, duties, gross monthly salary) - Wage compliance declaration (the employer certifies that the salary is not below Swiss market levels) - Certificate of good conduct (for some sectors) - Completed official cantonal forms in German or Italian
### Crucial deadlines for renewal Submit the renewal application at least 30 days before the expiration date. If it expires without renewal, the right of residence ceases immediately: the worker must leave Switzerland or submit a new application for a permit (L or B, depending on the conditions).
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to verify that the proposed salary meets Swiss standards for your sector. Consult the [LAMal information](nav:health) to understand your health insurance obligations (mandatory even with an L permit, to be arranged within 3 months of arrival). Administrative clarity from the start simplifies future renewals and transitions to the B permit.

## In brief - The B residence permit is renewable in the Canton of Thurgau. - Requirements and documents vary depending on the case. - The renewal procedure is handled by the cantonal migration office.
## Key facts - **What**: B residence permit in the Canton of Thurgau. - When: Not specified. - Where: Canton of Thurgau. - Who: Cantonal migration office. - Amount: Not specified.
The B residence permit in the Canton of Thurgau is an essential document for foreign residents who wish to settle in Switzerland for an extended period. This permit is renewable and requires compliance with certain requirements and the submission of specific documents. The renewal procedure is handled by the cantonal migration office, which is responsible for verifying compliance with current regulations.
### Requirements and Documents To obtain the B residence permit, it is necessary to meet a series of requirements that vary depending on the specific case. Among the required documents are a valid passport, a work contract, proof of accommodation, and, in some cases, a certificate of good conduct. It is essential to verify the specific requirements applicable to your case with the cantonal migration office.
### Duration and Renewal The B residence permit has a limited duration and must be renewed periodically. The renewal procedure involves submitting an application to the cantonal migration office, accompanied by the necessary documents. It is important to respect the deadlines and provide all the requested information to avoid delays or complications in the procedure.
### Concrete Examples For example, an Italian citizen working in Frauenfeld, the capital of the Canton of Thurgau, must present a valid work contract for at least six months and proof of accommodation, such as a rental contract. If the work contract is for one year, the B residence permit can be automatically renewed for the same duration, provided there are no significant changes in the applicant's circumstances.
### Regulations and Deadlines According to the Federal Law on Foreign Nationals (LEStr) of December 16, 2005, the B residence permit can be renewed for periods of one or five years, at the discretion of the cantonal authorities. It is important to note that the renewal is not automatic and requires a new evaluation of the applicant's conditions. The fees for renewing the B residence permit in the Canton of Thurgau amount to CHF 100 for the annual renewal and CHF 200 for the five-year renewal.
### Operational Checklist 1. Verification of Requirements: Check the specific requirements for your case with the cantonal migration office. 2. Collection of Documents: Prepare all necessary documents, including passport, work contract, proof of accommodation, and certificate of good conduct. 3. Submission of Application: Submit the renewal application to the cantonal migration office with all required documents. 4. Payment of Fees: Pay the renewal fees, which vary depending on the duration of the permit requested. 5. Waiting for Decision: Wait for the decision of the cantonal authorities, which may take several weeks.

They will have to renew the B residence permit annually, unless they obtain a longer work contract.
### Conclusion The B residence permit in the Canton of Thurgau is a crucial document for foreign residents who wish to settle in Switzerland for an extended period. The renewal procedure requires compliance with specific requirements and the submission of accurate documents. By following the operational checklist and respecting the deadlines, applicants can facilitate the renewal process and ensure their legal stay in Switzerland.
> "The B residence permit is an important step towards integration in Switzerland. It is essential to follow the procedures carefully and respect the deadlines to avoid complications." - Cantonal migration office of the Canton of Thurgau ## Practical Implications The B residence permit has significant implications for foreign residents in Switzerland. This document allows them to settle in the country for an extended period, enabling them to work, study, and enjoy the services offered by Switzerland. However, it is important to comply with the requirements and deadlines to avoid legal issues. For example, an Italian citizen who wishes to move to Zurich must obtain the B residence permit and meet the specific requirements of the Canton of Zurich, such as demonstrating a minimum income of CHF 3,300 per month.
### Comparison with Other Permits The B residence permit is different from the L residence permit, which is valid for a shorter period and is not renewable. Additionally, the B residence permit is an intermediate step towards the C residence permit, which offers greater rights and benefits to foreign residents. For example, the C residence permit allows living in Switzerland without time limits and participating in municipal elections.
### Hypothetical Scenarios Suppose a cross-border worker wishes to move to Switzerland to work. In this case, they will need to obtain the B residence permit and meet the specific requirements of the Canton of Thurgau. Once the permit is obtained, they can settle in the country and enjoy the services offered by Switzerland. For example, a French citizen working in Geneva must obtain the B residence permit and meet the specific requirements of the Canton of Geneva, such as demonstrating a minimum income of CHF 3,500 per month.
### Operational Checklist - **Required Documentation**: Valid passport, employment contract, residence certificate, certificate of good conduct. - Economic Requirements: Demonstrate a minimum income of CHF 3,300 per month for the Canton of Zurich and CHF 3,500 per month for the Canton of Geneva. - Deadlines: Submit the renewal application at least 30 days before the current permit expires. - Costs: The fee for renewing the B residence permit is CHF 100.
### Regulations and Dates The Federal Act on Foreign Nationals and Integration (LEI) of December 16, 2005, regulates residence permits in Switzerland. According to Article 31 of the LEI, the B residence permit can be renewed if the applicant meets certain requirements, such as economic capacity and social integration.
### Concrete Examples A German citizen working in Bern obtained the B residence permit in 2020. They met the specific requirements of the Canton of Bern, such as demonstrating a minimum income of CHF 3,400 per month. In 2023, they renewed the permit without issues, thanks to their economic capacity and social integration.
### Comparison of Practical Scenarios - Scenario 1: An Italian citizen working in Zurich obtains the B residence permit and meets the specific requirements of the Canton of Zurich. After five years, they can apply for the C residence permit. - Scenario 2: A French citizen working in Geneva obtains the B residence permit and meets the specific requirements of the Canton of Geneva. After five years, they can apply for the C residence permit.
### Conclusion The B residence permit is a fundamental document for foreign residents in Switzerland. Compliance with requirements and deadlines is essential to avoid legal issues and enjoy the services offered by the country.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Renewal Procedure The renewal procedure for the B residence permit in Switzerland involves submitting an application to the cantonal migration office. It is crucial to respect the deadlines and provide all necessary documents to avoid delays or complications. The cantonal migration office will verify compliance with current regulations and issue the permit renewal.
### Step-by-Step 1. Check the specific requirements applicable to your case. - For example, in the Canton of Zurich, a valid work contract for at least six months and proof of accommodation are required. 2. **Prepare all necessary documents**, including: - Valid passport with at least six months of remaining validity. - Work contract or employment letter. - Proof of accommodation (rental contract or property certificate). - Certificate of good conduct. - Financial documentation demonstrating the ability to support oneself economically (e.g., bank statement with a minimum balance of CHF 10,000). 3. Submit the renewal application to the cantonal migration office. - In the Canton of Bern, the application can be submitted online via the official portal. 4. Wait for verification by the cantonal migration office. - The process can take up to three months, so it is advisable to start the procedure well in advance. 5. Receive the renewed B residence permit. - Once the application is approved, the renewed permit will be sent by mail or can be picked up at the cantonal office.
### Operational Checklist - Check specific cantonal requirements. - Prepare necessary documents: - Valid passport. - Work contract. - Proof of accommodation. - Certificate of good conduct. - Financial documentation. - Submit the application: - Online or in person at the cantonal office. - Wait for verification: - Average processing time: 3 months. - Pick up the renewed permit.
### Useful Tools For further information and to manage the renewal procedure, you can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF/EUR comparator](nav:exchange) available on the site. These tools can help you better understand the financial implications and plan the permit renewal.
### Comparisons between Practical Scenarios - Scenario 1: Renewal without complications - An Italian citizen residing in Geneva submits the renewal application with all necessary documents and a valid work contract for one year. The procedure is completed in two months. - Scenario 2: Renewal with incomplete documentation - A French citizen residing in Basel submits the renewal application but forgets to include the certificate of good conduct. The procedure is delayed by one month until the missing document is submitted.
### Regulations and Dates - Federal Law on the Residence and Settlement of Foreigners (LDSE) - Effective from January 1, 2008. - Article 32: Renewal of the B residence permit. - Fees - Cost of renewing the B residence permit: CHF 100. - Cost of the certificate of good conduct: CHF 20.
### Concrete Examples - Case 1: Renewal in Zurich - An Italian engineer submits the renewal application with a valid work contract for 12 months and a rental contract in Zurich. The procedure is completed in two months. - Case 2: Renewal in Bern - A French doctor submits the renewal application with a valid work contract for 6 months and proof of accommodation in Bern. The procedure is completed in three months.
### Conclusion Renewing the B residence permit in Switzerland requires attention to detail and the preparation of all necessary documents. By following the step-by-step procedure and using the available tools, it is possible to complete the renewal without complications.

item.title: Wages and the labour market in Aargau: sectors and levels
item.description: In the canton of Aargau, salaries vary for training and collective agreements. Learn about pay differentials, social contributions, and federal labor protections.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss salaries vary by education; no federal minimum - Social contributions: AVS/AI 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LPP 7-18% depending on age - Aargau applies federal law with protections common to all of Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss salary structure and labor market - When: Current regulations until 2026 - Where: Canton of Aargau, Switzerland - Who: Employees and private employers - Hours: 45 hours/week (industry) or 50 hours (other sectors)
In the canton of Aargau, as in all of Switzerland, the labor market is based on specialized training and differentiated salary levels according to the level of education. Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage; wage conditions are regulated by collective labor agreements and specific cantonal ordinances. In Aargau, common federal standards apply: a maximum of 45 hours per week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 hours for other sectors, a minimum of 4 weeks of vacation, and notice periods according to seniority (1 month in the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth, and 3 months from the tenth).
### Three levels of training and salary differentials
Training in Switzerland follows three paths: apprenticeship (AFC — Federal Certificate of Competence, usually 3-4 years), secondary education (post-compulsory diploma), and tertiary education (university, polytechnics). Each level opens different segments of the labor market with different remunerations. An apprentice receives a lower initial remuneration; a graduate accesses technical or employment roles with average remuneration; a graduate qualifies for managerial or specialist positions. In the canton of Aargau, the distribution of the workforce by sector (manufacturing, services, trade) reflects this training hierarchy: industrial and manufacturing sectors primarily seek candidates with AFC and higher diplomas.
### Social contributions on salary
Every employee in Switzerland automatically pays social contributions from their gross salary: - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% of gross salary (the employer pays an equivalent amount) - Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): 1.1% up to the annual maximum - Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA): 0.7–1.5% depending on the economic sector (employer's responsibility) - Pension fund (LPP): 7% (25-34 years), 10% (35-44), 15% (45-54), 18% (55+ years) on coordinated salary
These charges reduce the net amount compared to the gross salary. Additionally, the employee privately pays for health insurance (LAMal), which is not deducted from the paycheck.
### Collective agreements and minimum wages
In Switzerland, there is no uniform federal minimum wage. Collective labor agreements (CCL), negotiated between unions and employers' associations, define the guaranteed minimum wages and employment conditions for each sector. In the canton of Aargau, the sectors with the highest incidence of CCL are metalworking, construction, and public services. An employee hired under a CCL receives at least the minimum wage provided; those working without an applicable CCL risk receiving a lower wage, unless protected by a specific cantonal ordinance. ### How Gross and Net Salary Work
When an employer and an employee negotiate a 'gross salary', they are agreeing on an amount that already includes mandatory social contributions. The employee does not pay the AVS separately; the employer withholds it directly from the paycheck along with income taxes (federal, cantonal, and communal). The net salary for the employee = gross salary - AVS/AI/IPG (5.3%) - AD/AC (1.1%) - LPP (7-18% depending on age) - federal and cantonal/communal taxes - LAMal (paid directly by the employee).
A hypothetical scenario: An employee in Aargau with a gross annual salary of CHF 60,000 sees approximately 5.3% withheld for AVS/AI (CHF 3,180), 1.1% for AD/AC (CHF 660), plus federal and cantonal taxes according to the communal residence. Adding the LPP quota (7-18% depending on age: for example, 10% for a thirty-five-year-old, CHF 6,000), the net salary drops to about 40-50% of the gross salary — a significant reduction due to contributions and taxes.
### Salary Differential by Sector and Qualification
The three training tracks create substantial salary differentials. An apprentice with a Federal Vocational Education and Training (VET) certificate (18-22 years) receives lower remuneration, typically in the range of CHF 800-1,500 monthly depending on the sector. A post-compulsory education graduate accesses positions as an employee, technician, or maintenance worker, with gross salaries averaging CHF 3,500-5,500 monthly. A university or polytechnic graduate qualifies for roles as an analyst, engineer, coordinator, or manager, with salaries of CHF 6,000-10,000+ monthly. These differentials widen with seniority: with the same qualification, a worker with 10 years of experience typically earns 20-40% more than a new hire.
In the canton of Aargau, industrial sectors (metalworking, pharmaceuticals, chemicals) offer above-average national salaries. Sectors with lower added value (retail, catering, cleaning services) offer lower remuneration, even with the same qualification. This differential reflects market demand: rare skills find greater salary compensation.
### Impact and Value of Collective Agreements
Collective labor agreements (CLAs) are in force in about half of the Swiss private sectors. In Aargau, sectors such as metalworking, construction, public services, and transportation have strong CLAs. An employee covered by a CLA benefits from a guaranteed minimum wage, automatic seniority supplements, cost-of-living allowances, family allowances for dependents, and greater protection against arbitrary dismissal. Those working without an applicable CLA depend on cantonal law and their own position: they may earn more if their qualification is rare, or less if their position is vulnerable.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to get information on salaries and contracts in Aargau
If you are a candidate or a worker looking for information on average salaries and collective agreements in the canton of Aargau, there are reliable resources available:
1. **SECO Portal** (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, www.seco.admin.ch): publishes statistics on the Swiss labor market, median salaries by profession and canton, unemployment rate. You can filter the results by canton (Aargau) and economic sector.
2. Collective agreements database: SECO maintains a searchable operation of current CBA in Switzerland, with full texts available for download. By accessing the portal, you can search by canton (Aargau) and sector to verify if a CBA covers you and what the negotiated minimum wages are.
3. Aargau Cantonal Labor Office (Department of Economy, Labor Market): provides free advice on federal and cantonal labor rights, contacts of trade unions and professional associations, mediation in case of wage disputes.
4. Trade unions and professional associations: Swiss trade unions (VSA, OCST, UNIA, Syndicom, etc.) negotiate CBAs and can inform you if your sector has an applicable collective agreement and what your exact rights are.
### What to check before accepting a job offer
Before signing a contract in Aargau, check:
1. Applicability of a CBA: Ask the employer if your role is covered by a collective agreement. If so, the offered salary MUST comply with the minimum wage specified by the CBA; if lower, it represents a violation.
2. Net salary calculation: Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) provided by Frontaliere Ticino to accurately estimate the net amount based on the proposed gross salary, according to Aargau taxation and your personal data (marital status, children, canton of residence).
3. Salary components: Distinguish between base salary, seniority supplements, family allowances (if CBA), company benefits (supplementary pension, life insurance, extra leave). Request a written copy of the salary structure.
4. Probationary period: The contract must specify the probationary period (maximum 3 months for dependent work), during which both parties can terminate with 7 days' notice. After the probationary period, notice periods increase to 1 month (first year).
### If your salary is illegal
If you believe your salary violates an applicable collective agreement or cantonal minimum regulation, you can:
1. Administrative appeal: Contact the Aargau Cantonal Labor Office with written proof of the violation (contract, pay slip, applicable CBA). The office will mediate and may order the payment of the difference.
2. Union arbitration: If you are a member of a union, you can request arbitration through the union representation, at no personal cost.
3. Civil lawsuit: File a lawsuit with the cantonal court within one year of receiving the salary. Recommended with legal assistance.
### Final CTA
To accurately calculate your monthly and annual net salary in Aargau, including all deductions (AVS, AD/AC, LPP, federal/cantonal/communal taxes, LAMal), access the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) of Frontaliere Ticino — a free tool that allows you to enter the agreed gross salary, canton of residence, tax year, and obtain a detailed estimate of the pay slip and monthly nets.

item.title: Aargau: salaries, sectors and levels of training
item.description: How salaries are structured in Aargau according to the degree of training, the sectors they hire and the collective agreements envisaged.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, some cantons have one. - Salary levels depend on education, sector, experience. - Collective agreements set minimum wages by sector. - Maximum working hours 45-50 hours/week, minimum holidays 4 weeks.
## Key facts - **What**: Salary structure in Aargau according to education and sector - When: System in place for all of 2026 - Where: Canton of Aargau, Switzerland - Who: Private and public employees - Maximum hours: 45-50 hours/week - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks per year (5 for under 20s) - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% employee's share - Maternity: 14 weeks at 80%
The labor market in the canton of Aargau follows the federal Swiss rules for determining wages, supplemented by cantonal regulations. Unlike some European countries, Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage: wage determination occurs through collective labor agreements (CLA) and company agreements.
### Salary Structure by Education Level
Salary levels in Aargau are strongly correlated with professional education level. Apprentices in vocational training (VET — Federal Vocational Baccalaureate) have salary scales defined by CLAs and progress from the first to the third year of apprenticeship. A vocational training diploma accesses positions of skilled worker or clerk, with higher compensation than apprentices. Holders of higher specialist diplomas (federal exams) or university degrees receive even higher compensation.
The salary structure reflects the educational investment: an engineering graduate earns on average more than a technical profession graduate, who in turn earns more than an apprentice. Collective contracts specify minimum wages for each education level and professional category.
### Collective Agreements and Hiring Sectors
In Aargau, as in all of Switzerland, the main hiring sectors are manufacturing and industry (pharmaceuticals, chemicals, machinery), finance and insurance, retail and wholesale trade, construction and real estate, healthcare and social services, technology and telecommunications.
Each sector has its own collective agreements defining minimum wages, benefits, and working conditions. For example, the pharmaceutical sector has generally higher wage standards than retail trade.
### Working Conditions and Mandatory Contributions
The maximum working hours in Switzerland are set at 45 hours per week in the industrial and office sectors, and 50 hours in other sectors. The minimum guaranteed holidays are 4 weeks per year (5 for employees under 20). The employer must also pay mandatory contributions: 10.6% for AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer), 1.1% for unemployment contributions (AD/AC) up to the annual maximum, and LAINF/LAA contributions (0.7–1.5% depending on the sector) for accident insurance.
Maternity is covered for 14 weeks at 80% of salary (loss of earnings compensation — IPG), while paternity is guaranteed for 2 weeks. Trial periods in contracts are typically 1-3 months. Determining the right salary for a position in Aargau requires considering several factors beyond the level of education. Professional experience, technical specialization, managerial responsibility, and the company context influence the final compensation.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). If you are looking for a job in Aargau or evaluating a salary offer, here are the concrete steps to verify if the compensation is adequate and which tools to use.

### Step 1: Identify the applicable collective agreement
The first step is to identify the collective agreement (CA) that applies to the role and sector. Most positions in Aargau fall under a specific sector CA (e.g., CA for chemistry, pharmaceuticals, metallurgy, commerce). You can find the text of the contract on the company's website offering the job, on the website of the sector's employers' association, or at the Aargau cantonal employment office.
The CA defines the minimum salary for your level of education and professional category. If the offer is below the CA minimum, it could be a sign of contractual issues.

### Step 2: Compare with the market using the calculator
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to verify the average salary range for your profession, level of education, experience, Aargau canton, and sector. Enter the profession (e.g., 'mechanical engineer', 'nurse', 'software analyst'), years of experience, level of education (apprenticeship, CFC diploma, higher specialist, degree), sector (manufacturing, healthcare, technology, etc.), and Aargau canton.
The tool returns the national and cantonal median salary, allowing you to position the offer relative to the market.

### Step 3: Calculate net salary and tax situation
A crucial aspect often overlooked: the gross salary does not correspond to the net amount available. Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to quantify the tax impact: the federal direct tax (FDT) represents about 8-12% of the gross (varies with income, age, marital status), to which is added the Aargau cantonal tax (varies with the specific municipality), municipal tax, AVS/AI/IPG contributions 5.3%, unemployment contributions (AD/AC) 1.1% up to the maximum, and LAINF/LAA contributions 0.7–1.5% (deducted by the employer).
Example: a gross annual salary of CHF 80,000 could result in a net monthly salary of CHF 4,800–5,100, depending on personal and municipal situation.

### Step 4: Evaluate additional benefits
In addition to the base salary, many companies offer contributions to the pension fund (LPP) above the legal minimum, bonuses and 13th salary, supplementary health insurance ([health insurance](nav:health) with reduced deductible), additional leave beyond the legal minimum (4 weeks), smart working and flexibility, continuous training.
These elements increase the overall value of the offer even if the base gross appears modest.

### Step 5: Check notice periods and the first year
If you accept a job in Aargau, note that the probationary period is usually 1-3 months with a notice period of 1 week or 1 month. After the first year, the notice period becomes 1 month. From the 10th year of service with the same employer, the notice period increases to 3 months. This means that the first years represent a higher risk of unexpected termination.
For any doubts about contracts, salaries, termination rights, contact the Aargau cantonal employment office or an independent labor consultant. Consultation is often free at public offices.

item.title: Kindergarten Bern: fees, costs and subsidies
item.description: Child care in the canton of Bern: kindergartens, Tagesfamilien, after-school. Rates calculated on family income and available cantonal subsidies.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Childcare is a cantonal responsibility in Switzerland - Fees vary based on family income - Cantonal subsidies reduce costs for families - Options: daycare centers, Tagesfamilien, after-school programs
## Key facts - **What**: Childcare services in the canton of Bern - When: From birth (daycare centers) to school age - Where: Canton of Bern, Switzerland (cantonal/communal management) - Who: Cantonal administration, municipalities, public/private facilities - How: Fees calculated based on income, subsidies available
Childcare in Switzerland is not a federal responsibility but a cantonal one. In the canton of Bern, families have several options to balance professional commitments with childcare: daycare centers (Kindertagesstätten), Tagesfamilien (day families), and after-school programs (Hort). The fees for these services are not fixed at the national level but vary from canton to canton and, within the canton of Bern, from municipality to municipality.
A distinctive feature of the Bernese system is the calculation of fees based on family income. This means that the cost of childcare depends on the family's economic situation: parents with higher incomes pay higher contributions, while those with lower incomes benefit from reduced fees. It is a progressive mechanism aimed at making the service accessible to all segments of the population.
The cantonal administration of Bern also offers dedicated subsidies to reduce the economic burden. These contributions are intended for families that meet specific income criteria and represent a crucial element of the cantonal and communal welfare system.
### Types of available services
In the canton of Bern, the range of solutions is wide. Daycare centers welcome children from birth to 4-5 years old, with flexible hours (full-time, part-time, by days). Tagesfamilien are professionals who welcome a limited number of children at their home, under the supervision of the cantonal administration and the municipality. After-school programs cater to school-age children and offer afternoon care and care during holidays. Each service has its own cost structure and specific access criteria defined by the municipality of residence.
### How fees are calculated
In the canton of Bern, the cantonal administration sets the general principles, but it is the municipalities that define the specific fees for childcare services in their territory. The calculation takes into account mainly the gross family income: the higher the income, the higher the contribution tends to be. This progressivity ensures that the cost remains accessible even to families with limited economic resources. In addition to income, other factors can influence: the number of children in care simultaneously, the hours and days of attendance, the age of the child. There is no single fee for the entire canton; each municipality has management autonomy.
Cantonal and municipal subsidies are added to the progressive fee system. A family that meets certain income criteria can benefit from contributions that cover part of the costs. The goal is to ensure that childcare does not represent an economic obstacle for those who work and have a family.
### Procedure to access services
Families looking for a place in a daycare center or after-school program should contact the competent office of their municipality of residence. Each municipality in the canton of Bern has a contact person for childcare. It is advisable to inquire in advance about available places, as in many municipalities the demand exceeds the supply. The registration procedure and times vary from municipality to municipality, as do the priority criteria. ## Economic implications for families The cost of childcare has a significant impact on the family budget. In the canton of Bern, as in the rest of Switzerland, a family with both parents working and a young child in daycare faces the central question: is professional childcare economically sustainable? The answer depends mainly on two factors: the family's gross income and the amount of available subsidies.
### How subsidies reduce the burden Imagine a family with a substantial total annual gross income. Without subsidies, the fee calculated on income could result in a significant monthly contribution to daycare. However, if the municipality applies subsidy criteria and the family meets the parameters (number of children, financial situation, etc.), the actual contribution could be significantly reduced. This is where the cantonal and municipal policies supporting families make a concrete difference: subsidies are the main tool to ensure fair access to childcare.
### Comparison between services Another factor to consider: which service to choose between daycare, Tagesfamilien, and after-school care? Daycares often have more standardized fees, regulated by both the canton and the municipality. Tagesfamilien can sometimes offer slightly different fees and greater hourly flexibility, but they vary greatly depending on the individual provider. After-school care, being a service for older children and therefore with lower costs than daycares, can represent a less costly solution for those with school-aged children.
### Tax deductions An often overlooked aspect: external childcare expenses can have tax implications. In many Swiss cantons, including the canton of Bern, documented childcare expenses are partially or fully deductible from taxable income. In the Bernese context, it is advisable to verify with the cantonal tax office or the municipality which expenses are recognized as deductible and to what extent. This element further reduces the net burden on the family and represents a concrete opportunity for tax savings.
### When to start the search Experience in Bernese municipalities shows that the demand for daycare places often exceeds the available supply. It is advisable to start the search well in advance (even 6-12 months before the desired start date). At the same time, it is recommended to request information on available subsidies for your situation: some municipalities publish online simulators, others require direct contact with the office.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## How to access childcare services in the canton of Bern
Those interested in enrolling a child in a childcare service in the canton of Bern must follow a series of concrete steps. The procedure begins with the search and selection of the facility, proceeds with the registration, and concludes with the signing of the contract and the start of the service.
### Step 1: Inform yourself at the municipality
The first step is to contact the municipal office responsible for childcare (often part of the family services office or the social services department). Here you can obtain a list of accredited facilities — public and private daycare centers, Tagesfamilien, after-school programs. Each municipality usually also publishes information on tenders, registration deadlines, and waiting lists, often available online.
### Step 2: Check access criteria and simulate costs
Before registering, it is essential to request a fee simulation. The municipal office can calculate the required contribution based on the declared family income. This is the time to ask which subsidies the family might be eligible for and how to apply for them. This data allows for a realistic economic evaluation and a conscious choice.
### Step 3: Apply and wait for the response
Once the preferred facility has been identified, the family submits the registration application according to the municipality's procedures (paper form or online platform). Many municipalities have specific registration periods (e.g., spring for the following school or calendar year). If the application is accepted, the contract with the facility follows, where payment methods and attendance conditions are defined.
### Step 4: Apply for cantonal subsidies
Parallel to the registration with the facility, the family must apply for a subsidy with the municipality and/or the canton if they believe they are entitled to it. The criteria and required documentation (income certificates, bank statements, tax returns) vary, but the municipal office provides the complete checklist. The subsidy approval times can range from a few weeks to a few months; it is best to submit the application as soon as possible.
### Step 5: Annual planning
Once registered and receiving the subsidy, the family must stay informed about any changes in fees (usually annual) and subsidy criteria. It is advisable to recertify the income each year and check if the economic situation allows the subsidy to be maintained. Contact [nav:cost-of-living](#) to compare the cost of living in the canton and plan the overall family budget.
Timely planning and quick requests to the municipalities significantly increase the chances of obtaining a place in a quality facility and fully benefiting from the available subsidies in the Bernese system.
